product.title: Mongolian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Mongolian (Khalkha, Cyrillic script): a stressed pronunciation guide printed right above every word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Mongolian builds its sentences back to front, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet table, the rules of vowel harmony, a summary of the seven cases, A1 verb tables, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the verb that always stands at the end of the sentence to the one sound rule that decides the shape of almost every suffix.

blocks.text: Mongolian is spoken by about six million people — three million in Mongolia itself, the rest in Inner Mongolia in northern China and in Russia. That number is small, and that is exactly its charm: there are almost no foreign speakers. Mongolians who hear a foreigner say one whole sentence in their language react the way you would if a tourist suddenly spoke your hometown dialect perfectly.

This course writes Mongolian in **Cyrillic script**, as Mongolia uses it today. The beautiful vertical Mongolian script — written top to bottom — is being revived and has been compulsory in schools since 2025, but newspapers, signs, phones, and all everyday conversation still use Cyrillic. You'll learn Cyrillic first, and that's the right call.
Why Mongolian is friendlier than you expect
Four things make the road shorter than you'd think. All four are worth knowing from the first page, because together they will save you months.

items: **Verbs don't change with the subject.** One form for I, you, he, we, they — not even the English *-s* of "she goes". Compare Russian, with six forms per verb. In Mongolian, *би явна* and *тэд явна* use exactly the same verb.
**No gender, no articles.** No *der/die/das*, no *a/the*. *Ном* can mean "book", "a book", or "the book" — context decides.
**Spelling is almost entirely faithful to sound.** One letter, one sound. After the next two pages, you'll be able to read signs in Ulaanbaatar correctly, even before you know what they mean.
**Nouns usually don't change for plural in everyday use.** *Хоёр ном* = "two book", not "two books". The number is enough.

blocks.text: So where's the hard part?
In three places, and all three are genuinely new to you. It's better to know what they look like now, so they don't surprise you later.

items: **The verb stands at the end of the sentence.** Mongolian builds sentences back to front from an English point of view: "I at home rice eat." This isn't a rule to memorize but a habit of the ear — it's worked on from Unit 6 and repeated in every unit after that.

**Vowel harmony.** The vowels in one word must belong to one group, and suffixes adjust to match. "At home" is *гэрт*, "in the city" is *хотод* — the same suffix, a different sound. The rule takes one paragraph and is in the front pages; using it takes twenty units.
**Seven cases** — or, to give them a more honest name, seven **prepositions glued to the end of the word**. English writes "at home"; Mongolian writes *гэрт*. Same content; it just moves to the back.

blocks.text: Notice that none of the three is a long list to memorize. All three are habits — things that grow from use, not from rereading explanations. That's why the explanations in this course are deliberately short. The long part is the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: This course asks one thing of you: **read out loud**. Mongolian long and short vowels can't be learned with your eyes. If you read silently, you're learning a different language.
Each unit is designed for **one sitting, 20–30 minutes**. Twenty units means about a month if you sit down five times a week. Don't do two units a day; what counts isn't speed but the number of days.
**Don't memorize the tables.** Tables in this course are for looking things up, not for learning by heart. What you memorize are whole sentences from the dialogues.
If a grammar note feels too heavy, **just skip it**. It will come back in a later unit in a lighter form.

blocks.text: The three lines under each dialogue sentence

The first line is the Mongolian sentence, with the pronunciation printed small right above each word. The second line is a natural English translation. The third line is the **word-for-word translation**, including the suffixes.

blocks.title: Example
items: *Би гэрт байна.*
I'm at home.
I home-at is.

blocks.text: That third line is the most valuable one, and the one people skip most often. It shows that *гэрт* isn't a new word but *гэр* (home) with "at" stuck on the back — and that the verb *байна* really does stand at the end, not in the middle. Once you get used to reading the third line, the seven Mongolian cases stop feeling like seven things to memorize and start feeling like a list of prepositions that have moved.
Symbols used

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: The part under discussion — usually the suffix that changes.
The strongest syllable. In Mongolian it falls on the first long vowel; if there's no long vowel, on the first syllable.
The consonant before it is softened — the sound of *ь*. The tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth, a bit like the "n" in British "new".
A spot that English speakers often get wrong.

blocks.text: The Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet is the Russian Cyrillic alphabet plus **two letters** Russian doesn't have: **Өө** and **Үү**. Both are vowels, both are common, and both are sounds English doesn't have. Everything else is exactly like Russian Cyrillic.

The good news: of those thirty-five letters, **ten already look familiar** because they resemble Latin letters and sound the same or nearly the same (**А, Е, К, М, О, Т, Э** and friends), **six are deceptive** because they look Latin but sound different (**В, Н, Р, С, У, Х**), and the rest are completely new. The completely new ones are actually the quickest to learn, because no old habit gets in the way.

blocks.title: ⚠️ The six letters that trip people up most
items: **В в** is read **v** (sometimes w), not *b*. *Ванна* = *VAN-na* (bathtub).
**Н н** is read **n**, not *h*. *Нар* = *nar* (sun).
**Р р** is read as a rolled **r**, not *p*. *Ром* = *rom*.
**С с** is read **s**, not *c*. *Сар* = *sar* (moon, month).
**У у** is read **u** as in "put", not *y*. And the look-alike **Ү ү** sounds different — see below.
**Х х** is read **kh**, with friction in the throat like the "ch" in Scottish "loch", not *x*.

blocks.text: Two letters only Mongolian has

head: Letter
How to make it
Example
Meaning
rows: Round your lips as if to say **o**, then say **e** (as in "bed") without changing the shape of your lips. Same as German *ö*.
Round your lips as if to say **u**, then say **i** (as in "machine") without changing the shape of your lips. Same as German *ü*.

blocks.text: ⚠️ These two letters **change meaning**; they're not decoration. *Ор* (enter) vs *өр* (debt); *ус* (water) vs *үс* (hair). If you say *ү* as a plain *u*, you're not speaking with an accent — you're saying a different word. Practice both in front of a mirror now, for five minutes, then move on.
Long vowels: written twice, held twice as long

A vowel written double is long, and length changes meaning: *цаг* (tsag, time) vs *цаас* (TSAAS, paper); *ор* (or, come in!) vs *оор* (not a word). The rule is simple and reliable: **one letter, one beat; two letters, two beats.** The pronunciation guide doubles long vowels too (aa, ii, uu, öö, üü) — except two: long *оо* is written **ō** and long *ээ* is written **ē**, because "oo" and "ee" would trick English eyes into "food" and "see". English doesn't mark vowel length in spelling at all, so this is the first ear habit you need to build.

blocks.title: Four pairs to practice today
items: *цаг* (time) — *цаас* (paper)
*сар* (moon) — *саар* (to milk)
*ор* (enter) — *өр* (debt)
*ус* (water) — *үс* (hair)

blocks.text: Read this table aloud once from top to bottom, then close it. Don't memorize it — the letters will memorize themselves over the twenty units ahead. In the pronunciation: a as in "father", e as in "bed" (written **eh** at the end of a syllable, so you neither drop it nor read it as "ee"), i as in "machine", o as in "law" but short, u as in "put", kh as in "loch", j as in "jam", dz as in "adze", ts as in "cats".

blocks.title: Four unwritten sound habits
items: **Short vowels in non-first syllables almost disappear.** *Байна* sounds like *BAI-n*, *сайхан* like *SAI-khn*, *морин* like *MO-rin* with a very thin *i*. The pronunciation guide in this course writes them in full so you know the spelling, but your ear will hear them clipped.
**Г at the end of a word sounds like a soft *k*.** *Цаг* sounds like *tsak*, *ног* like *nok*. This is never written.

**Mongolian Л isn't an ordinary *l*** — the tongue touches the roof of the mouth, but air escapes at the sides with friction, like *l* and *sh* at once (close to Welsh *ll*). It's fine to use a plain *l* at first; people will still understand.
**A word with Ө or Ү will never contain А, О, or У** — that's a result of vowel harmony on the next page, and it holds for almost every native Mongolian word.

front.title: Vowel harmony: one rule that governs everything

blocks.text: This is the most important page of the whole front section. If you only have time for one page, choose this one. Vowel harmony decides the shape of almost **every suffix** in Mongolian — possessive, location, object, time, all of them. The rule is one paragraph; the payoff lasts as long as the language.
Mongolian vowels fall into two groups

head: Group
Its vowels
Example words
rows: *их* (much) — goes with the other vowels in the same word

blocks.text: **The rule:** in a single word, the vowels can come from only one group. No native Mongolian word contains both *о* and *ө*, or both *а* and *э*. And — this is the important part — **suffixes adjust to the group of the word they attach to.**

Notice that the suffix is **the same** in all four rows — only the color of the vowel changes. "From" is always *-VVс*, with V following the group; "by, with" is always *-VVр*. Once you see it as one suffix with a changing vowel, rather than three different suffixes, the amount you have to memorize drops to a third.

blocks.title: How to use it in practice
items: Look at the **last vowel** of the base word. If it's *а, о, у* → use *а* or *о* in the suffix. If it's *э, ө, ү* → use *э* or *ө*.
If the last vowel is just *и*, look at the vowel before it. *Ном* → back. *Хичээл* (lesson) → front, because it has *э*.
If the word contains **only** *и* (*мий*, *чи*), treat it as **front group**.
⚠️ Loanwords from Russian and English often break this rule (*телевизор*, *компьютер*). Don't let them confuse you — they're guests, not natives.

blocks.text: One last thing that makes this feel much lighter than it sounds: **you don't have to decide anything while speaking.** Vowel harmony is standardized mouth laziness — your mouth simply prefers to keep going with the shape it's already using rather than jump. After five units, your hand will write *гэрт* and not *гэрд* without thinking, because *гэрд* will feel wrong on your tongue.

Mongolian is a long way from English — no family relationship at all. But it has borrowed from sources English knows well: Russian during the twentieth century, English through technology, and a small number of words from Sanskrit and Tibetan through Buddhism. As a result, there are a couple of hundred words you'll recognize as soon as you see them.
Through Russian and other European languages
Through Sanskrit and Buddhism

This group is interesting because some of its words reached English too, by a completely different route — *guru* and *lama* are English words today. The forms changed at both ends, but they still recognize each other.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Six words that look familiar but mean something else
items: *ном* (nom) = **BOOK**, nothing to do with eating.
*сар* (sar) = **MOON / MONTH** (in the sky and on the calendar), not "sir".
*бор* (bor) = **BROWN**, not "bore".
*бас* (bas) = **ALSO**, not "bass". "Bag" is *цүнх* (tsünkh).
*мал* (mal) = **LIVESTOCK**, not "mall". It's one of the most important words in Mongolian.
*хар* (khar) = **BLACK**, not "car". "Day" is *өдөр* (ödör).

blocks.text: Finally, one word you must know before Unit 1: **ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ** — or in Cyrillic, *Монгол*. It's read *MON-gol*, and it's more than the name of a country. It's the name of the language, the people, and the adjective all at once: *монгол хэл* (the Mongolian language), *монгол хүн* (a Mongolian person), *Монгол Улс* (the State of Mongolia). ⚠️ Note that it's written with a **small letter** when it means the language or the people, and with a capital only as part of the country's name — the opposite of English.

blocks.text: Choosing the suffix form

blocks.title: Four things that save beginners
items: **The suffix -т is used after hard consonants** (*в, г, с, р, л, м, н* in some words), **-д after the rest.** If in doubt, say both out loud — the right one feels lighter on the tongue. People still understand if you get it wrong.

**An indefinite object takes NO suffix.** *Би ном уншина* = "I read a book (any book)". *Би номыг уншина* = "I read the book". This is the one place where Mongolian marks what English marks with *a* and *the*.
**"To have" isn't a verb.** It's the suffix *-тай*: *Би нохойтой* — "I have a dog", literally "I dog-with".
**Stacked suffixes follow a fixed order:** base + plural + case + possessive. *Найз-ууд-даа* — "to my own friends".

blocks.text: This is Mongolian's biggest gift: **not a single form on this page changes with the subject.** One form covers I, you, he, we, you all, and they. What you have to choose is not who's doing it, but **when** and **how sure** you are.

blocks.title: Negation — three words, three places
items: **-гүй** attaches to verbs: *явахгүй* (won't go), *сайхан**гүй*** — ⚠️ not used for adjectives; use *биш* for those.
**биш** negates nouns and adjectives: *Би багш **биш**.* — I'm not a teacher.
**үгүй** stands alone as the answer "no": *Үгүй, би мэдэхгүй.* — No, I don't know.
**байхгүй** = "there isn't", the opposite of *байна*: *Мөнгө **байхгүй**.* — There's no money.

blocks.text: Numbers 0–20
Tens, hundreds, thousands

blocks.title: ⚠️ Numbers have two faces
items: Standing alone (counting, phone numbers, prices): *нэг, хоёр, гурав, дөрөв, тав…*

Before a noun, the form gets shorter: *нэг ном*, *хоёр ном*, ***гурван*** *ном*, ***дөрвөн*** *ном*, ***таван*** *ном*, ***зургаан*** *ном*, ***долоон*** *ном*, ***найман*** *ном*, ***есөн*** *ном*, ***арван*** *ном*.
The pattern: stand-alone form + **-н**. *гурав* → *гурван*. Only *нэг*, *хоёр*, and *хорь* → *хорин* need separate attention.
**The noun stays singular.** *Гурван ном* = "three book", never "three books" — like "three sheep" in English.

blocks.text: Days and time

⚠️ These day names come from Tibetan and name **seven heavenly bodies**, just like the day names in Japanese and Sanskrit — and like English *Sunday*, *Monday*, and *Saturday*. So you can memorize them as one series, not seven separate words.
Personal pronouns in their four most common forms
⚠️ **Тэр means both "he" and "she"** — there's no choosing between them. *Тэр* also means "that" — context tells them apart, and the context is never ambiguous.
Possessive suffixes — the everyday way

That last suffix — *-аа* and its relatives — has no direct equivalent in English and is used very often. It means "belonging to the subject of this sentence, whoever that is". *Тэр ээж**дээ** ярьсан* = "She spoke to **her own** mother". With *түүний ээжид*, the meaning shifts to **someone else's** mother.
Question words

blocks.title: ⚠️ Every question needs the particle вэ or бэ
items: Mongolian questions **end with a particle**, and you mustn't forget it: without the particle, your sentence sounds left hanging.
**вэ** is used after vowels and after *н, л, м, в*: *Чи хаана байна **вэ**?*
**бэ** is used after other consonants: *Энэ юу **вэ**?* — ⚠️ *юу* ends in a vowel, so *вэ*. An example with *бэ*: *Хэд **бэ**?*
For yes/no questions, the particle is **уу / үү / юу / юү**, following vowel harmony: *Та багш **уу**?* — Are you a teacher?

blocks.text: The words you'll need most at A1, in English alphabetical order. The strongest syllable is marked with capitals in the pronunciation.

If you've reached this page after working through twenty units, you now have something real: Mongolian Cyrillic you can read without spelling it out, around three hundred active words, the seven cases in the singular, present and past verbs, vowel harmony that's starting to run by itself, and the ability to handle everyday business — introducing yourself, ordering, asking the way, shopping, telling the story of your day. That's real A1, not A1 only on the cover.
Three most useful things to do now

items: **Reread all the dialogues from Unit 1 onward, in order, over two days.** Unit 1 will feel almost silly easy — proof that the course works. More importantly, you'll catch patterns you didn't see the first time, especially the word order that once felt backwards.

**Start writing five sentences a day about your own day.** Not exercises from a book: sentences about your life. *Өнөөдөр би гэртээ ажилласан. Оройн хоолондоо мах идсэн.* The mistakes that show up there are your real mistakes, and those are the fastest to fix.

**Find someone to talk to before you feel ready.** There will never be a "ready" moment. Three hundred words are enough for a first halting conversation, and halting conversations are what carry you to A2. Mongolians almost never meet foreigners who speak their language; their patience with beginners is nearly endless.

blocks.text: What's waiting at A2

head: Topic
Why it comes next
rows: Linking two events in one sentence: "after eating, I left". This is what makes sentences start to sound grown-up.
*Найзынхаа гэрт* — "at my own friend's place". Three suffixes in one word, and Mongolians use them every day.
*-гдах* and *-уулах*: "be read", "make someone read". One root, four meanings.
*Уншдаг хүн* — "a person who reads (habitually)". Mongolian puts the whole relative clause in front of the noun.
Compulsory in Mongolian schools since 2025. Once you're strong in Cyrillic, this script becomes a gift, not a burden.

blocks.title: A word before we part
items: Mongolian pays you back quickly. Because the verbs don't change and there's no gender, your first correct sentence will come in the second week — much sooner than with any European language. What's slow is the ear: it takes months before clipped short vowels stop sounding like fog.
*Амжилт хүсье!* (AM-jilt KHÜS-yeh) — Good luck!
*Баяртай!* (ba-YAR-tai) — Goodbye!
